content:
The reform (in force 1 January 2023, applying to deaths from that date) is essentially a rollback of Switzerland's "forced heirship" system. Swiss law has long guaranteed certain close relatives a minimum slice of the estate — the *compulsory share* (Pflichtteil) — no matter what your will says. The revision shrank the list of people who can claim one.

**Children: essentially unchanged**
- Children and other descendants still have a compulsory share equal to **¾ of their statutory share** (what they'd inherit if you died without a will).
- Example: one child, no spouse → the child's statutory share is the whole estate, so they can always claim at least ¾. You can freely give away ¼ (to a charity, a friend, an unmarried partner, etc.).
- One practical change that affects them: lifetime gifts made **more than 5 years before your death** no longer count when their claim is calculated. Under the old rules, gifts made to deliberately cut out an heir could be chased indefinitely. So an early transfer (e.g., signing your flat over to your child now while keeping the right to live there) becomes "safe" after five years.

**Parents: lost their compulsory share (the headline change)**
- Before 2023, if you died without descendants, your parents could claim **half of their statutory share** regardless of your will.
- Now they have no claim at all. If you're childless, you can leave everything to whomever you want and disinherit parents and siblings entirely. (The grandparents' old special claim — the "Vorschlag" — was abolished too.)
- Note: dying *without* a will is unchanged — parents still inherit under the statutory order. The change only matters when a will or gifts bypass them.

**Spouses/registered partners: unchanged** — still ½ of their statutory share protected. (Unmarried partners still get nothing by law, which is worth knowing.)

**The freely disposable portion (freie Quote)**

It's not a fixed percentage — it's whatever remains after the compulsory shares are satisfied:

> freely disposable portion = estate − sum of all compulsory shares

Because the compulsory shares depend on who survives you, the free portion varies:
- **Married, two children:** spouse ¼ compulsory, children 3⁄8 combined → free portion **3⁄8** (37.5%). Identical to before the reform.
- **Married, no children:** spouse ¼ compulsory → free portion **¾** (was 5⁄8 before).
- **Single, no children:** free portion **100%** (was ½ if a parent was still alive).

So the often-quoted "more testamentary freedom" really only benefits people *without* descendants. If you have children, your freedom is what it always was.

**A few things worth knowing for a future will**
- The compulsory share is a **money claim**, not a right to specific assets — a shortchanged child can demand the difference in cash from the heirs, not the house itself.
- Nothing happens automatically: a compulsory heir who's shortchanged must actively claim it (generally within a year of learning of it, ten years at the latest).
- You can't will your way around the system — the only levers are shrinking the estate during your lifetime (gifts that age past the 5-year mark) or getting a compulsory heir to sign a waiver contract, usually in exchange for compensation.
- A will written entirely by hand, dated and signed is valid in Switzerland, but for property, a business, or a blended family, a notarised will or inheritance contract is far safer.

This is general background rather than advice — but for casual planning purposes: childless people got much more freedom; parents lost their safety net; children's protection stayed put.

**Draft:**

Short context: Swiss inheritance law has long had "compulsory shares" (Pflichtteile): minimum portions that certain close relatives can claim even against your will. The reform, in force 1 January 2023 (revised Swiss Civil Code), cut these back.

**Children: essentially unchanged**
- Children and other descendants still have a compulsory share equal to 3/4 of what they would inherit by law (their "statutory share").
- If you have one child and no spouse, the child's statutory share is the whole estate, so they can claim at least 3/4; you can freely dispose of 1/4 (e.g., to a charity, a friend, an unmarried partner).
- One practical difference: lifetime gifts you made more than 5 years before your death no longer count when your compulsory heirs calculate their claims. Under the old rules, gifts intended to "cut out" an heir could be counted indefinitely. So a large early gift (e.g., transferring your flat to your child while keeping a right to live there) becomes safe after five years.

**Parents: lost their compulsory share (the headline change)**
- Until 2023, if you died without descendants, your parents could claim half of their statutory share no matter what your will said.
- Since 1 January 2023, they have no claim at all. If you have no children, you can now leave your entire estate to anyone — partner, friends, charities — and disinherit parents and siblings completely.
- Intestacy didn't change: if you die without a will, parents still inherit under the statutory order. The change only bites when there's a will (or gifts) that circumvents them.
- The grandparents' old special claim ("Vorschlag" — a claim limited to assets they had given you) was also abolished.

**Spouses/registered partners: unchanged**
- 1/2 of statutory share protected. (Unmarried partners still have no claim and no intestate share — worth remembering.)

**The freely disposable portion (freie Quote)**
It's not a fixed fraction — it's whatever is left after the compulsory shares are satisfied:
freely disposable portion = estate − sum of compulsory shares.

Examples (estates and fractions):
- Married, two children: statutory shares — spouse 1/2, each child 1/4. Compulsory — spouse 1/4, each child 3/16 (total 3/8). Free portion = 3/8, i.e., 37.5%. (Same as before the reform.)
- Single, no children: now 100% free (previously 50% if a parent was alive).
- Married, no children: spouse's compulsory share is 1/4, so 3/4 free (previously 5/8).

Important: the compulsory share is a *money* claim against the heirs, not a right to specific assets (the house, the company). And nothing happens automatically — if a child gets less than their compulsory share, they must actively claim the difference (generally within a year of learning of it, ten years at the latest).

**Practical notes for a future will**
- No will → statutory succession, unchanged by the reform.
- You can't "will around" compulsory shares; you can only shrink the estate in advance (gifts that age past five years) or get a compulsory heir to sign a waiver contract (usually against compensation).
- A will entirely handwritten, dated and signed is valid in Switzerland (holographic will), but for real estate, businesses, or blended families, a notarised will or inheritance contract is much safer.

Caveat: general info for deaths on/after 1 Jan 2023, not legal advice.
